sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No. The third card, "Sketches", starts at about x 174 while the other four start at x 160. It shares their right edge at about x 918, so it is also about 14 px narrower. It spans roughly y 356–456. The viewer's eye trips there, and they have to decide whether "Sketches" is a sub-step of "Research" or a layout slip. The offset is small enough to look like a mistake rather than a choice, but large enough to suggest nesting. Either reading costs a second look, and the nesting reading changes what the list says about the project's structure. Source: Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*: elements of one kind share one style and spacing, and a variant appears only where the rules call for it. Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I: a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver. Fix: put the card back on the shared left edge at x 160 and full width. If Sketches really is a sub-step of Research, show that on purpose: indent it by a clearly larger step, tie it visibly to its parent, and apply the same rule to any other sub-steps. Defect. Weight: major. It is the one thing that breaks an otherwise orderly list, and it is the first thing a careful reader notices.
2. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. Each of the five cards sits inside its own near-black outline, which looks about 3 px thick (x 160–920, from y 120 to y 692). Together the outlines are the darkest, heaviest marks on the page, heavier than the stage names inside them. The page reads as a stack of boxed compartments rather than a sequence of stages. The roughly 18 px gaps between cards already separate them, so the outlines add weight without adding meaning. Source: Lupton, *Thinking with Type*: rules and boxes should show relationships, "not trap each entry inside a heavily guarded cell". Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 4–5, on non-data ink. Fix (approved direction): remove the borders, or replace them with space or a pale tone, so the lines do not compete with the content. Convention. Weight: minor. The page still works, but it looks heavier and more like a template than it needs to.

**What's working.** The copy is tight and finished. Each card pairs a one-word stage name with a sentence that starts with a verb and says who does what: "Visit three sites and write up what the teams there need." A stranger could follow the plan without filling any gaps. The type, the single dark neutral color and the plain rectangles also share one sober mood that suits an internal planning note.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere; every element, rule, box and ornament does a job)

**First read:** My eye lands on "Project notes" at the top left, then runs down a stack of five boxes with the same heavy outline. The "Sketches" box (y≈356–456) starts about 14 px further right than the others. That makes it look like a sub-step of Research, or like a slip. It reads as a short list of project stages in a docs or notes tool, and it feels plain and orderly.

**Job (assumed):** A notes page that lists the stages of a design project in order, for the team working on it.

**Walk: What matters first**
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. "Project notes" (about 32 px, bold, at y≈55–90) is the biggest and heaviest text. The dark 3 px box outlines are loud, but they don't compete with it as a starting point.
- Each text level can be told apart at a glance: **yes**. There are three sizes: title about 32 px, card headings about 20 px, body about 16 px. The steps between them are clear.
- Headings differ in more than size: **yes**. Card headings are bold and body text is regular.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Clear starting point:** "Project notes" is the only text at about 32 px bold, set alone above the stack with about 30 px of space under it. The eye knows where to start, and the page has one clear top level.
- **Clean three-level scale:** title about 32 px, card headings about 20 px bold, descriptions about 16 px regular. The steps are big and size works together with weight, so each card's name stands out from its sentence without any extra styling.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

*Note for the director:* the "Sketches" card is indented about 14 px (its left edge is at x≈174, the others at x≈160). That reads as a hierarchy signal, as if Sketches were a sub-step of Research, but none of this section's lines covers it. It belongs under arrangement/alignment. If the indent isn't meant to show nesting, it gives the viewer a false hierarchy. The heavy, identical 3 px outlines on all five cards also make the stack louder than its content needs. That is a taste point for arrangement or color, not a failure here.

I critiqued the arrangement section from the full image only: Bash was refused, so I ran neither the crop script nor the entries script, and I read the layout entries directly. The image is about one screen, so crops would not have changed what I saw.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Blocks don't share one grid, and one element misses an alignment by a few pixels** (checklist lines "Do all blocks… take their edges… from one grid" and "Is every element either exactly aligned… or clearly off it, with no near-misses"):
   - **Where:** the third card, "Sketches" (about x 174–918, y 356–455). Its left edge sits about 14 px to the right of the shared left edge at x≈160 that the title and the other four cards use. Its heading and body text move with it, to x≈201 instead of x≈187. Its right edge stays at x≈918 like the others, so the card is not shifted but narrowed: 14 px shorter on the left only.
   - **What the viewer gets:** the eye catches on the third card on the way down. The offset is too big to miss and too small to read as meant, so the viewer has to decide whether it is a bug or a meaning. The likely wrong reading is that "Sketches" is a sub-step of "Research", nested under it. Nothing else supports that reading: it has the same heading style, the same box, the same 18 px gaps, and it is one stage in a run of five. The viewer gets a hierarchy the content doesn't have, or concludes the page is unfinished.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, says every block takes its edges from one grid. Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance", says a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver and the whole look unfinished. Gerstner's point that repeated elements follow one program applies too: one card in a matched set breaks the pattern.
   - **Fix:** put the card back on the x≈160 edge so all five cards share both edges. If "Sketches" really is a sub-step of "Research", make the break decisive: indent it by at least the cards' inner text margin, so its box lines up with the text above at x≈187, and add a second sign such as a smaller heading or a lighter border, so the nesting reads as meant.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect. Major: on a page this sparse, alignment is most of the design, and this one mistake changes how the list of stages reads.

**What's working.**
- **Even spacing.** The gaps between the cards are one interval, about 18 px, all the way down. Each heading sits tight on its own line of text, well inside the card, so every card reads as one unit and the five read as an even sequence. That evenness is exactly why the one inset card stands out, so keep it when the alignment is fixed.
- **Open space.** The empty space is gathered into one large block to the right of the column (about x 920–1280) and a band at the bottom, not scattered into small gaps. The column reads as a calm, document-style list with clear margins on every side.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid governs the page; exactly aligned or clearly off, no near-misses).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Each card title is a single bold word at about 20 px, with a regular one-line note under it in the same family. Weight does the ranking and size stays close, so every card reads as one unit and the list scans in a single downward pass. This is "bolder, not bigger" (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*).
- The type scale has three clear levels (page heading about 34 px, card title about 20 px, note about 16 px) in one sans family, with dark text on white. Nothing collides and nothing looks faint.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is entirely neutral: white ground, dark slate card borders, near-black text.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The piece sticks to one neutral range with no added hue. That suits a plain project-notes list: nothing competes with the words, and the structure reads fully on value alone, so it also holds up in grayscale and for color-blind viewers. The heading and body text are near-black on white, which looks well above 4.5:1, so the text is easy to read.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied, so I judged from the whole image only. At about 1280×800 it is roughly one screen, so I would not have needed crops anyway.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
